claim.why_it_matters: This page carries a TWO-level index nesting ('Numeric-edited category' > 'Category of data' > 'Numeric-edited 162') and the markdown flattens both levels to flush left, along with every other sub-entry on the page (Object, Object orientation, Operators, OPTIONAL phrase, ON SIZE ERROR phrase, etc.). Three distinct index levels collapse into one, which changes what the index asserts.

verdict.reasoning: REJECTED as a ledgerable discrepancy, though the observation itself is factually accurate. Verified by rendering spec_p1251.png at 300 dpi and reading the glyph positions directly. (1) The claim's premise is TRUE: page 1251 (printed folio 1221) does print three distinct indent columns. In the 300-dpi render, 'Numeric-edited category  165, 379, 446' starts at the same left margin as 'NUMERIC phrase', 'NUMERIC-EDITED' and 'Numeric-edited data item  165'; 'Category of data' starts one indent stop in, at the same x as 'CLASS clause  194, 382' and 'INITIALIZE statement  637'; and 'Numeric-edited  162' starts at a THIRD, deeper stop. Both quotations in the claim are accurate transcriptions of their respective sources. (2) But the difference is leading whitespace and nothing else. A line-by-line comparison of the full page - both columns, all ~110 entries from 'Floating-point 109' through 'ORD function 900' - shows every index term, every comma-separated page number, and every entry's ORDER reproduced verbatim in the markdown. Nothing is missing, nothing is added, nothing is reordered, and nothing is relocated. The 'misplaced-content' kind label is therefore wrong on its face: no content is misplaced, it is all exactly where the PDF puts it, minus the indent. The only textual nit on the whole page is unrelated to this claim ('OCCURS ... DEPENDING clause' for the PDF's ellipsis glyph). (3) This is not a page-1251 defect at all - it is a uniform whole-index transcription convention. Bucketing every indented line in specs/ISO_COBOL.md by 5000-line region shows indented lines throughout the normative body (53 through line 5000, 103, 156, 165, 173, 217, 183, 103, 293, 367 ... up through the 45000 bucket) and then exactly ZERO indented lines anywhere from line 50000 to EOF at 53204 - i.e. across the entire alphabetical index, roughly printed pages 1230-1260+. A direct scan (awk over lines 51000-53204 for /^[ \t]+[A-Za-z]/) returns 0 hits. Ledgering this per page would mint ~30 duplicate findings for one global whitespace convention. Notably the transcription DOES preserve indentation where it encodes normative structure - lettered sub-rules such as '   a)' / '   b)' in the general and syntax rules survive intact - so no normative nesting is at risk. (4) The affected material is non-normative back matter. The alphabetical index is navigational apparatus; no conformance requirement, syntax rule or general rule derives from index nesting, so no compiler behavior can be mis-derived from the flattening. The navigational function is in fact fully preserved and arguably improved: every page number is rendered as a live '#page-N' anchor, so a reader looking up 'Numeric-edited' still lands on page 162. Under the stated rejection criteria the 'missing' text is present, the difference is formatting-only, and it does not change any assertion the standard makes.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. The claim's factual observation is correct - the PDF prints three indent levels on this page ('Numeric-edited category' flush left, 'Category of data' one stop in, 'Numeric-edited 162' two stops in) and the markdown renders all index lines flush left - but the finding is misclassified and mis-scoped. Correctly stated it is: 'the markdown transcription drops leading indentation throughout the entire alphabetical index (~pages 1230-1260+, zero indented lines from md line 50000 to EOF), losing the visual parent-child encoding of index sub-entries.' It is cosmetic/navigational, not structural: all index terms, page references and their order are transcribed verbatim; page numbers are preserved as live anchors; indentation IS retained where it carries normative meaning (lettered sub-rules in the body); and the index is non-normative back matter from which no compiler behavior is derived. If tracked at all it belongs as a single global note on index formatting, not as a per-page structural discrepancy.
